strengths: CheckEval addresses an important NLP evaluation problem: sensitivity to the choice of judge model. Its checklist approach is simple, requires no evaluator training, and makes the contributions of individual criteria to the final score inspectable.

The experiments cover 12 open and proprietary models across SummEval, Topical-Chat, and QAGS. Reported improvements in human correlation are substantial for several weaker evaluators: Llama3.1-8B improves from approximately 0.24 to 0.41 Spearman correlation on SummEval and from 0.11 to 0.46 on Topical-Chat.
The paper includes useful human validation, augmentation/filtering ablations, alternative aggregation experiments, and controls involving binarized baseline outputs and increased inference budget.

The three-stage pipeline is clearly presented. Seed questions, prompt templates, model identifiers, decoding settings, computational costs, and a code link provide a useful foundation for reproducibility.
weaknesses: The central agreement analysis contains a serious unresolved numerical inconsistency. Table 14 reports Krippendorff’s alpha = 0.0090 and Fleiss’ kappa = 0.5749 for binarized G-Eval outputs in the Large group. For the same complete binary rating matrix, standard versions of these coefficients should differ only by a small finite-sample correction. The discrepancy suggests different inputs or an implementation problem. The authors should specify the rating matrices, agreement units, distance functions, and missing-output handling, and audit the calculations. Because the headline reliability improvement depends on these results, this is the decisive reason for recommending revision next cycle.

The agreement comparison needs a clearer common measurement basis. It is unclear whether CheckEval agreement concerns individual checklist answers or aggregated text scores. Pooling heterogeneous questions can capture shared question-specific answer tendencies without establishing comparable agreement on text quality. Report agreement both within questions and on final scores. Moreover, Appendix C.3 overstates the remaining advantage: for the Topical-Chat Top-3 group, binarized G-Eval achieves kappa = 0.5806 versus CheckEval’s 0.5736, contradicting the claim of a large remaining gap across every group.

Checklist alignment with the intended constructs is not consistently convincing. Table 26 rewards using the source’s terminology or jargon under relevance, which can penalize valid paraphrases. Table 27’s groundedness questions emphasize conversational relevance and consistency without explicitly checking support from the supplied fact. These concerns have empirical consequences: CheckEval’s SummEval relevance Spearman correlation is lower than G-Eval’s for nine of twelve models, despite very high reported agreement on that dimension. This deserves direct analysis.

Statistical support is insufficient for several improvement claims. The strongest-model differences are sometimes small, such as SummEval Spearman 0.5486 versus SEEval’s 0.5377 and Topical-Chat 0.6451 versus G-Eval’s 0.6389. Paired confidence intervals respecting shared documents or conversations are needed. The additional human correlation study uses only 20 stratified summaries, while the 100-summary agreement study covers only relevance. The pooled six-rater kappa of 0.49 also does not separately establish agreement between humans and LLMs.

Numerical reporting needs reconciliation before the results can be reproduced confidently. For example, SEEval with Gemma2-9B has SummEval Spearman 0.49 in Table 1 but 0.4269 in Table 22. The Topical-Chat mean Spearman/Pearson labels in Table 15 also appear reversed relative to Table 24. These discrepancies should be corrected alongside the agreement audit.
